extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public seeking moral/social guidance (early 18th-century style)
extracted.subtask_description: Periodical moral essays offering norms for conduct, style, and temper — e.g., on sharing knowledge, clear writing, candour, and the value of cheerfulness versus transient mirth. Advice is framed for a general reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of communicating knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Against the maxim that 'A Man's Knowledge is worth nothing, if he communicates what he knows to any one besides,' the essay argues that communicating knowledge is a natural pleasure and virtue: 'There is certainly no more sensible Pleasure to a good-natur'd Man, than if he can by any means gratify or inform the Mind of another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share discoveries and thoughts publicly rather than hoarding them; the act of putting ideas into words clarifies them and rewards the communicator through improvement and pleasure. Beware narrow spirits who prefer secrets reserved for elites; transparency and teaching are portrayed as socially and personally beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity over affected obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of writing unintelligibly as a mark of reputation is condemned: some authors 'affect Obscurity' so that few can comprehend them, and some moderns 'write without any Meaning at all' by 'throwing so many Words at a venture' and leaving readers to 'find out the Meaning of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deliberate obscurity or abstruse mannerisms intended to burnish reputation. Good writing should convey meaning clearly; obscurity used to create an aura of superiority is an anti-pattern and is criticised as dishonest or lazy workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerfulness is superior to mirth
rubrics_metrics.description: Chearfulness (habit) is distinguished from Mirth (act): 'Mirth is short and transient. Chearfulness fixed and permanent.' Cheerfulness is a stable temper that prevents deep melancholy, whereas mirth produces fleeting transport and may be followed by depression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate steady cheerfulness rather than seeking brief fits of mirth. As a lasting habit, cheerfulness preserves judgement and emotional equilibrium and is ethically preferable to wanton or excessive laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold benefits of cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider cheerfulness 'with regard to ourselves, to those we converse with, and to the great Author of our Being.' As to self: clarity of imagination and undisturbed judgement; to others: produces love and good-will; to God/Providence: an implicit praise and gratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or cultivating a cheerful temper, note its effects across these three relations: personal mental health and faculties, social influence (affability and generating goodwill), and spiritual/grateful posture toward Providence. Examples and descriptions of each effect are given in the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate limits to cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two stated conditions that can reasonably deprive a person of cheerfulness: 'The first of these is the Sense of Guilt... The second... is Atheism.' Other hardships (pain, sickness, poverty, old age, even death) are regarded as bearable by a virtuous mind and not grounds to abandon cheerfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between moral/spiritual reasons (guilt, disbelief) that undermine cheerfulness legitimately, and external misfortunes that a virtuous person should meet with fortitude and equanimity. This is a normative test for the authenticity of cheerfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour in admitting faults
rubrics_metrics.description: An ingenuous acknowledgment of a fault is praised as making amends and even expiating the fault: 'All such Miscarriages as flow from Inadvertency are more than repaid by it.' Genuine confession or apology restores relations and demonstrates character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage sincere acknowledgments of error (distinguish from token or insincere apologies). Examples (private notices, public acts of contrition) are used to show how candour disarms resentment and is a mark of greatness rather than weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors/publishers are morally advised to be honest about their role: 'it would not hurt the reputed Author of that Paper to own, that of the most beautiful Pieces under his Title, he is barely the Publisher.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take credit only for what one actually performs; claiming undue authorship undermines self-respect and honesty. This functions as a norm for ethical conduct in literary or public attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid token or theatrical devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of those 'very zealous and punctual to perform an Ejaculation that is only preparatory to the Service of the Church, and yet neglect to join in the Service it self.' Holding a hat, bowing, or other perfunctory gestures without participation is called out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against superficial religious behaviour (performative piety). True devotion requires participation and sincerity rather than the mere observance of external signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer employing wounded veterans
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir Roger's remark: 'I never make use of any body to row me, that has not either lost a Leg or an Arm. I would rather bate him a few Strokes of his Oar, than not employ an honest Man that has been wounded in the Queen's Service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates a social practice of preferring those injured in service for employment as a moral economy of gratitude and public virtue. Presented as a gentlemanly norm and an instance of practical benevolence.
